value.0: There's the champion the book says you are. The backrooms are shut, the maiming bill is ash, and my fighters walk to the ring without signing away their knees. You did that. Drinks are on the house forever, and the house means me.

Hold up. Let me look at you. Reach, decent. Footwork, honest. Spearwork, not finished, and I don't book unfinished fighters anywhere near what's behind that wall. Wring the last drop out of your training first. When the spear's got nothing left to teach you, my door knows your name.

Turn around, slow. Reach, footwork, price. I size everybody, don't be flattered. Here's the situation. Somebody's running maiming bouts off my book, behind my own club. Backroom circuit, no medics, no rules, and they're teaching a guard that doesn't just stop a swing, it collects on it. Their adepts run the sign-up rooms. Put six of them down and lift the Crippling Defense Backroom Bout Ledger they book fights on. The bookmakers won't move against the circuit without paper, and that ledger is the paper.

Signed. Freight corridor, the door that isn't there, six adepts, and the Crippling Defense Backroom Bout Ledger off their booking table. Don't wreck the ledger swinging. It's worth more than the six of them stacked.

Crippling Defense. The proper version's a thing of beauty. A guard that taxes every swing thrown against it, until the other fighter's paying rent just to keep his arms up. You'll learn it, that's the purse at the end of all this. The backroom version skips the discipline and goes straight for the tendons. Career-enders, every bout. That's what I want gone.

Behind the club, down the freight corridor, there's a door the club pretends isn't there. A key opens it, and the key's yours the minute you sign with me. Past that door it's their territory, the whole warren of backrooms. My name's worth nothing in there, so don't spend it.

The adepts are young, hungry, and they've been sparring career-enders for months. They come in low, work the knees, and they don't stop when you're down, because nobody ever taught them to. Keep your feet wide and your temper cold. And if a fight feels easy, it's an audition. Theirs.
That ledger's still taking bets on maiming bouts, which means every day you dawdle, somebody's career ends in a back room. Six adepts. Go.
You're moving like a man who won six times tonight. Table's clear. Let's see the paper.

Look at this. Forty bouts a month, half of them ending careers, all of it booked in my club's shadow. The bookmakers are going to choke. Here's your purse, clean credits, counted twice. And you just went from sign-up to fighter in my book. Stay there.

The ledger did its work, but the circuit answered by rigging the rings themselves. Their specialists fitted shock plates under the backroom canvases, and the regulator that runs them has been tampered so a bout can be tilted from the wall. Any fighter who won't throw a match gets the floor turned against him. Five specialists keep those rings humming. Drop them and pull the Crippling Defense Ring Shock Regulator out of the main pit's control box. With the tampered regulator on a table, the bookmakers can't call it rumor.
Good. Main pit control box, deep end of the warren. The regulator comes out whole, wires and all. It's evidence, not salvage. Five specialists will object. Overrule them.

Shock plates under the canvas, wired to a regulator in the control box. Legitimate clubs use them for training drills. Low current, teaches footwork. Theirs is re-wired to drop a fighter mid-exchange so the guard they're selling looks unbeatable. That's the con. Half that circuit's fearsome reputation is a dial on a wall.

Muscle I've got. Standing, I've got. What I don't have is jurisdiction. This is the Smuggler's Moon, nobody does. But bookmakers are the closest thing to law the fight trade answers to. They pull odds on the backroom circuit, the money dries up, and money's the one kind of blood that crowd can't afford to lose. Every job I hand you feeds their file.

The specialists are ring engineers who fight like fighters, because they were fighters. They'll pull you onto the plates and dance you around the dial. Watch the corners of the canvas. The seams show where the plates sit. Fight them on bare floor and it's just a fight, five times over.
Five specialists still running current under those rings, and every bout on plates is a fixed bout. Control box, main pit. The regulator, whole.
You smell like ozone. Good sign for us. Bad one for the circuit.

There's the con, in one ugly box. Rewired, re-dialed, maker's plate filed off, but the bookmakers' techs will read it like a bill. You've earned the purse and something better: my corner. From here up the jobs get heavier, and I don't send fighters I like into heavy jobs without saying so first.

Now the cage door. The champion pit sits behind a gate, and the gate has a warden. Old pit fighter, cracked his sigil the night he ended three careers in one bout. He holds that door for the whole circuit, and his guard is the real thing, the one we've been chasing this whole card. So listen, because this is how I corner fighters for champion bouts: nobody goes in alone. Three in the corner, always. That rule's older than you. Bring two you'd bleed for, put the warden down, and take the Crippling Defense Cracked Pit Sigil off him. The gate's authority dies with it.

Then go build your corner before you go anywhere near that gate. I've buried fighters who heard this speech and walked in solo anyway. Good ones. Better than you are this morning. Warden down, sigil off his neck, and all three of you walk back out. That's the whole card.

You've been fighting students of the guard. He's a source. Every swing you throw at him costs you. That's Crippling Defense done right: your offense becomes his purse. He'll let you spend yourself, then collect. The counter isn't cleverness, it's cash flow. Three fighters spending in turns, so nobody goes broke.

Twenty years of fight cards, and here's the arithmetic that survived them. One fighter against a champion is a payout for the house. Two is a puncher's chance. Three, rotating clean, resting in turns, is a plan. I have never once cornered a fighter alone for a bout like this, and I'm not starting with one I like. Two friends, or no fight.

The champion pit is a killing floor with a paying balcony. The crowd bets loud, the lights sit in your eyes, and the warden's crew works the rail. He'll offer to face you alone and make it sound like respect. The crowd loves that bit. It isn't respect, it's him picking the odds. Your corner is your answer. Keep them in it.
The warden still holds the cage door, and that cracked sigil still makes the circuit's word law past the gate. Get your two. Get it done.
The warren's gone quiet and the balcony crowd wants refunds. That's the sound a warden makes when he loses. Show me.

Ha! The bookmakers have wanted this sigil on a table for years. The gate's authority just became a souvenir. You and your corner did that, and don't let anybody, including me, talk about it like you did it solo. The purse is heavy this time. So is what comes next: the people who paid the warden's wages.

Behind every rigged circuit there's a table, and this one seats four. The promoters' inner circle. They set the bill, buy the wardens, and decide whose career ends on which night, all off my book and behind my club. One of them carries the Crippling Defense Promoter's Payout Chit, the marker their whole payroll runs on. All four go down and the chit comes to me. With it, the bookmakers freeze every account it touches, and the circuit can't pay a single door guard or dirty medic on this moon.

Then the card's set. Four promoters, wherever they're holed up in that warren, and the payout chit off whichever one carries it. My credits say the moneyman. When the table's cleared, come straight back. Don't stop to count anything you find down there. It's all counterfeit anyway.

A matchmaker who used to book for me, two enforcers who came up through the maiming bill, and a moneyman nobody's ever seen fight, which worries me more than the ones I have seen. They know the club, they know the warren, and by now they know your name. Treat every empty room down there like it's holding its breath.

Everything that circuit pays for, it pays through that marker. Door crews, crooked medics, the rail men, the silence. Kill the payroll and loyalty dies the same hour. This is the Smuggler's Moon. Four bodies get replaced by breakfast, but frozen money stays frozen. That's why I want the chit and the table both.

Not like fighters. Like a business protecting itself. Locked doors, bought crowds, the enforcers arriving while the moneyman runs your numbers from somewhere safe. Mind the corners and mind the exits. If your two from the warden bout still owe you a favor, this is a fine night to collect it.
The table's still seated and their payroll's still flowing. Four promoters and the chit. The longer they sit, the more doors their money buys.
Word beat you here. Four chairs, all empty. And your hand's in your pocket like it's holding something the bookmakers want.

That's the whole circuit's blood supply, right there in brass. The accounts freeze within the hour. You realize what's left, don't you. No adepts, no rigged rings, no warden, no table. Just the champion, sitting in the dark past the last gate, wearing the guard that started all this. Sit down before I offer you that one. I mean it.

Last name on the bill, and I'll say it plain, because you've earned plain. The champion down there is the guard. Crippling Defense, whole and perfected. The thing you've been climbing toward this entire card. Every fighter who ever swung on him retired the same night. That's not a figure of speech, I kept the book. He never rigged a ring or bought a table. He never had to. The circuit grew around him like scar tissue. There's no chit, no sigil, no paper to bring me this time. Him beaten is the proof, and the guard passes to whoever's still standing after. Take your corner, both of them. Nobody walks to that cage alone. Nobody ever has.

Then the card's printed. One bout, no purse I can pay that matches it, and the only belt is the guard itself. Corner tight, tempo yours. When it's done, walk back up here and let me be the first to say champion and mean it.

Once, up close, years back, when he was just a scary young spear on somebody else's card. A fighter twice his size threw forty strikes at him. He gave back six. The bout ended with the big man's arms dead at his sides and his career over, and the kid hadn't broken rhythm once. I signed him that night. That's my sin in all this, and it's why this last bout is personal bookkeeping.

A perfect guard has one cost: it only collects from what it can see. One spear, he reads forever. Three, rotating, no rhythm, no pride, and the tax spreads thin. Whoever he's facing spends careful while the other two spend loud. And when he opens the gap that says come win it alone, glory and all, you close ranks instead. Fall for that gap and I'm carrying three fighters home, not one.

Past the last gate there's no crowd, no lights, no book. Just a clean floor he keeps himself, and him standing on it like the fight already happened and you're late to it. Men come back from that room talking about how polite he was. They come back on stretchers, but they all mention polite. Go down as three, stay three, come home as three.
He's still down there, past the last gate, keeping that floor clean. Champions don't come upstairs. The bout happens when you and your corner walk down, not before.
The whole club went quiet an hour ago. Then the runners started shouting. I've promoted a thousand bouts and never once got to say this: the champion lost. Say the rest.

Then it's yours. The guard, the title nobody sane will challenge, and a fight trade on this moon that runs clean because you cleaned it. Crippling Defense, the real thing, earned the only way it ever passes: through it. I've cornered champions before, kid. I never once trained one I'd bet the club on. Book's closed. Go be unbeatable.
Go over the job once more.
Six adepts, one ledger. Put me on the card.
What kind of guard collects on a swing?
How do I get into the backrooms?
What are these adepts like in a fight?
I don't fight for free. Let me think on it.
The Crippling Defense Backroom Bout Ledger. Six adepts are off the card, permanently.
Run the ring job by me again.
Five specialists, one regulator. Consider the rings unplugged.
They're electrifying the rings?
Why do the bookmakers matter so much?
How do the specialists handle themselves?
My legs need a day. Then I'm in.
The Crippling Defense Ring Shock Regulator, wires and all. The rings fight fair now.
Talk me through the warden again.
Three of us, then. The warden's door comes open.
What makes his guard the real thing?
Why three in the corner?
What's the champion pit like?
I've got two names in mind. Give me time to call them.
The Crippling Defense Cracked Pit Sigil. He held the door. We held longer.
Deal me the table job again.
Four promoters, one chit. The table folds tonight.
Who sits at the table?
What can one chit really do?
How will four of them fight me?
After the warden, I need a breather. A short one.
The Crippling Defense Promoter's Payout Chit. The table's cleared and the payroll's dead.
Talk me through the champion again.
Then it's a title bout. Three of us walk down. I walk back champion.
You've seen him fight. Tell me.
How do I beat a perfect guard?
What's waiting past the last gate?
Not tonight. A title bout deserves my best, and my best needs rest.
It's over. The champion's guard broke, and all three of us walked out.
